[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Pagination Bottlenecks: OFFSET-FETCH vs. Keyset Pagination"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Pagination is a fundamental requirement in modern web and enterprise applications. However, as datasets grow into millions of rows, traditional pagination strategies can severely degrade database performance. This tutorial explores the architectural differences between OFFSET-FETCH (offset-based pagination) and Keyset Pagination (seek method), analyzing why bottlenecks occur and how to resolve them."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Problem with OFFSET-FETCH"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The OFFSET and FETCH clauses (or LIMIT and OFFSET in other dialects) are popular because of their simplicity. They allow developers to request a specific page number and size intuitively. However, the database engine executes these queries by scanning and discarding rows."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The database must read all preceding rows to determine the starting point of the requested page."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"I/O costs scale linearly O(N) with the page depth, meaning page 10,000 is exponentially slower than page 1."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"CPU utilization spikes due to unnecessary row evaluation and sorting operations."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Example: The OFFSET-FETCH Bottleneck"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"SELECT TransactionID, AccountID, Amount, TransactionDate
FROM FinancialTransactions
ORDER BY TransactionDate DESC, TransactionID DESC
OFFSET 100000 ROWS
FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the query above, even though only 50 rows are returned to the application, the storage engine must traverse and process 100,050 rows. If an index cannot fully cover this operation, it leads to massive bookmark lookups and disk reads."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"The Solution: Keyset Pagination (Seek Method)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Keyset pagination, often called the seek method, relies on the values of the last seen row (the keyset) to fetch the next set of results. Instead of telling the database to skip N rows, you tell it where to resume based on indexed columns."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Performance is O(1) relative to page depth; page 10,000 executes just as fast as page 1."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Utilizes B-Tree indexes efficiently to jump directly to the target leaf nodes."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Eliminates duplicate or missed rows caused by concurrent inserts or deletes during pagination."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Example: Keyset Pagination Implementation"},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"SELECT TOP 50 TransactionID, AccountID, Amount, TransactionDate
FROM FinancialTransactions
WHERE TransactionDate < '2023-10-01 12:00:00'
   OR (TransactionDate = '2023-10-01 12:00:00' AND TransactionID < 987654321)
ORDER BY TransactionDate DESC, TransactionID DESC;"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"To make Keyset Pagination perform optimally, you must ensure that your ordering columns are properly indexed. For the query above, a composite index on (TransactionDate DESC, TransactionID DESC) is mandatory."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use OFFSET-FETCH only for small datasets or admin interfaces where deep pagination is never expected."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement Keyset Pagination for high-throughput APIs, infinite scroll implementations, and large enterprise tables."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always include a unique tie-breaker column (such as a primary key) in your sort order and keyset logic to guarantee deterministic results."}]
